considered.name: DividendCutUnderCashStress
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dvt, at), 1)), INDICATOR(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dvt, at), 1)), 0)), RANK(NEG(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3))))
considered.hypothesis: Dividend reductions are informative only about the firms that cannot afford their commitment: a cut by a firm with weak multi-year operating cash flow reveals a binding internal funding shortfall and is followed by underperformance, whereas an equally large cut by a cash-generative firm is a discretionary reallocation toward investment or buybacks and carries no negative information.
considered.reasoning: The indicator restricts the financing leg to the positive part of the dividend decline, so dividend increases are set to zero rather than being mapped into the outperformance tail — this removes the internal inconsistency the critic identified while keeping the retrenchment channel that is otherwise absent from the archive. The magnitude of the cut interacts multiplicatively with cash-flow weakness, so the short leg is populated specifically by stressed cutters and healthy cutters sit in the neutral middle.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PerShareCashFlowVersusClaimBase
considered.expression: SUB(TS_RANK(RATIO(oancf, csho), 5), TS_RANK(csho, 5))
considered.hypothesis: Value accrues per claim, not per firm: a business whose operating cash flow per share stands near a five-year high while its share count is not at a historical peak is compounding internally, whereas a firm whose share count is at a record high while per-share cash generation sits near a low has expanded the claim base without delivering per-share quality, and the market underweights that arithmetic.
considered.reasoning: Both legs are within-firm historical ranks in the unit interval, so the two tails are economically explicit and symmetric — record-dilution-with-weak-per-share-cash-flow at the bottom, peak per-share cash flow with a stable claim base at the top — which fixes the sign contradiction of the earlier non-negative gate. It is not the net-share-issuance anomaly with a quality overlay: a heavy issuer whose cash flow grows faster than its share count still ranks high, so the signal prices dilution only when it is not accompanied by per-share quality gains.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: DeleveragingFundingSource
considered.expression: MUL(RATIO(dltr, at), SUB(RANK(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3)), RANK(RATIO(sstk, at))))
considered.hypothesis: Debt retirement means opposite things depending on its source: repaying maturing debt out of operating cash flow signals a business that has outgrown its leverage, whereas retiring debt with proceeds from selling equity is creditor-driven balance-sheet repair that transfers value from shareholders to bondholders.
considered.reasoning: CredibleDeleveraging failed on alpha (t 0.89) because its non-negative gate contrasted levered against unlevered firms — groups FF5 separates on its own — whereas here both legs are firms actively repaying debt and the contrast is purely the funding source, the feature that made BuybackFundingSource survive FF5. It extends the winning mechanism to a completely different financing action, so a positive result would establish funding-source credibility as a general principle rather than a buyback artifact.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: DebtRolloverChurnUnderIlliquidity
considered.expression: MUL(MIN(RATIO(dltis, at), RATIO(dltr, at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(act, lct), at))))
considered.hypothesis: Simultaneous large long-term borrowing and repayment is refinancing rather than net funding, and refinancing is a benign treasury operation for firms with a comfortable working-capital buffer but a symptom of maturity-wall pressure for firms whose current assets barely cover current liabilities.
considered.reasoning: The MIN of gross issuance and gross retirement measures rollover volume, a quantity that all net-debt-flow signals in the archive mechanically cancel, and the gate uses balance-sheet liquidity rather than profitability or cash flow, so it conditions on a quality dimension FF5 does not represent. This tests whether refinancing pressure — as opposed to net capital raising — is the part of the debt channel that carries return information.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: BuybackAtOwnCashFlowPeak
considered.expression: MUL(RATIO(prstkc, at), SUB(TS_RANK(RATIO(oancf, at), 5), RANK(RATIO(dltis, at))))
considered.hypothesis: A repurchase is credible when the firm is buying stock at a moment when its own cash generation is unusually strong by its own standards and it is not borrowing to do so; the same repurchase executed when internal cash flow is at a personal low and long-term debt is being drawn is balance-sheet engineering.
considered.reasoning: Rather than broadening the archive's best signal, this isolates the single design question its result leaves open — whether the alpha comes from the cross-sectional profitability rank (which is RMW-like and could be a factor artifact) or from the genuine funding-source contrast — by replacing the cross-sectional cash-flow rank with the firm's own five-year cash-flow position. If the alpha survives with a within-firm internal-funding measure, the mechanism is timing and funding credibility rather than a profitability tilt, which is the more valuable finding for the remaining generations.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: MultiYearSelfFundingGap
considered.expression: SUB(TS_SUM(RATIO(oancf, at), 5), TS_SUM(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at), 5))
considered.hypothesis: Over a full business cycle a firm either pays for itself or is paid for by the capital markets; the cumulative gap between five years of internally generated operating cash and five years of outside capital absorbed identifies durable self-funding franchises at one end and serial market-dependents at the other, a distinction investors underweight because it is invisible in any single year.
considered.reasoning: Expressing self-funding as a difference of asset-scaled cumulative flows rather than as a share removes the non-monotonicity the critic identified — there is no denominator that can approach zero or change sign, so the most cash-negative serial issuers now sit unambiguously at the bottom instead of wrapping around to the top. The five-year accumulation also makes portfolio membership slow-moving, which addresses the instability that has plagued the archive's one-year issuance sorts whose alphas evaporated under FF5.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ExpansionFundingSource
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(GROWTH(at, 1), INDICATOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 0)), SUB(RANK(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at))))
considered.hypothesis: Growth is not intrinsically good or bad; what matters is who paid for it. Expansion financed out of operating cash flow reflects a business reinvesting its own surplus, while identical expansion financed by outside capital reflects management appetite unconstrained by internal performance and is systematically overpriced at the time of the raise.
considered.reasoning: This moves the funding-source principle that produced the archive's only joint FMB-and-alpha result from the payout side to the investment side, a genuinely different economic decision, and it is not the accruals-times-issuance construction the critic identified as a re-test of DilutionQualityGate. The indicator restricts the action leg to firms that actually expanded, so both tails are growing firms distinguished only by funding source, while shrinking firms sit at zero in the middle rather than forming a tied mass in either leg.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: DividendHikeFundingSource
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(DELTA(RATIO(dvc, at), 1), INDICATOR(DELTA(RATIO(dvc, at), 1), 0)), SUB(RANK(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at))))
considered.hypothesis: Only firms generating internal cash can keep a raised dividend; a dividend increase declared in the same year the firm is tapping equity or debt markets is a signal-jamming gesture that is later reversed, whereas an increase paid from strong operating cash flow conveys sustainable earnings power.
considered.reasoning: Taking the positive part of the dividend change removes the incoherent quadrant the critic identified — externally funded cutters can no longer be pushed into the long leg, and internally funded cutters can no longer be shorted — so every firm in either tail is a dividend raiser and the sort is purely about how the raise was financed. Paired with the payout-level evidence already in the archive, it tests whether funding-source credibility operates on the news in a payout decision rather than on its level.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: RawSurplusGatedExpansion
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(GROWTH(at, 1), INDICATOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 0)), WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(oancf, at), RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at)), 1))
considered.hypothesis: What makes expansion credible is the actual cash surplus behind it — operating cash flow minus outside capital absorbed, measured in dollars per unit of assets — rather than the firm's relative standing on two separate cross-sectional rankings.
considered.reasoning: This isolates one design choice in the archive's best signal: the rank-difference gate is replaced by the economically literal funding surplus, which preserves magnitude information (a firm covering expansion twice over versus barely) that ranking discards, and simultaneously strips out the cross-sectional profitability rank that makes the current gate partly an RMW proxy. Comparing its alpha against ExpansionFundingSource tells us whether the winner's power comes from measured funding capacity or from relative-profitability sorting, which determines how the remaining generations should refine the gate.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ErraticFinancingWeakMargins
considered.expression: MUL(VOL(RATIO(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), ADD(prstkc, dltr)), at), 5), RANK(NEG(MA(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), at), 3))))
considered.hypothesis: A firm whose net capital flow swings violently from raising to returning and back has no stable financing policy, which in a low-gross-margin business signals that funding decisions are reactive to operating shortfalls rather than planned; such reactive financing predicts poor returns even when the average net flow is near zero.
considered.reasoning: This targets a quantity that every directional financing signal in the archive averages away — the instability of the policy rather than its direction — and gates it on gross margin, a quality dimension the archive has never used and which is not a cash-flow or distress proxy. It is the one exploratory slot in the batch, testing whether financing *variability* interacted with operating economics carries information distinct from financing level.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: DualChannelDeploymentFundingSource
considered.expression: MUL(SUMRANK(MUL(GROWTH(at, 1), INDICATOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 0)), RATIO(prstkc, at)), SUB(RANK(MA(RATIO(oancf, at), 3)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at))))
considered.hypothesis: Firms deploy capital either into the asset base or into retiring their own shares, and breadth across both channels is itself informative: a firm expanding and repurchasing simultaneously is making a wide commitment, and the credibility of that commitment depends entirely on whether operations or outside investors funded it.
considered.reasoning: Replacing the raw sum with SUMRANK puts asset growth and repurchase intensity on a common unit-interval footing, so the composite scale genuinely reflects deployment across both channels instead of being numerically swamped by asset growth as the critic noted. This makes it a real breadth test against ExpansionFundingSource: if the ranked dual-channel scale improves alpha and t-stat, deployment breadth adds information beyond the single strongest channel.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: FinancingRegimeGatedExpansion
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(GROWTH(at, 1), INDICATOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 0)), SUB(RANK(TS_SUM(RATIO(oancf, at), 3)), RANK(TS_SUM(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at), 3))))
considered.hypothesis: What the market misprices may be the firm's financing *regime* rather than this year's financing event: a firm that has covered its needs from operations for three straight years and now expands is a proven compounder, whereas a firm that has repeatedly returned to the capital markets is expanding on borrowed conviction even if this particular year's raise looks modest.
considered.reasoning: This is not a neutralization knob but a test of the economic horizon over which funding credibility operates — contemporaneous mix versus multi-year regime — and the archive gives a genuine reason to ask: the standalone five-year self-funding gap was weak (alpha 1.4%) while the one-year gate inside the expansion signal was strong, leaving open whether accumulating the gate helps or dilutes. A regime gate also changes portfolio membership slowly, which should improve the stability that one-year financing sorts have lacked.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: EarningsBackedVersusDepreciationBackedPayout
considered.expression: MUL(RATIO(ADD(prstkc, dvc), at), SUB(RANK(RATIO(ib, at)), RANK(RATIO(dp, at))))
considered.hypothesis: Distributions differ in what is behind the cash: payout supported by genuine bottom-line earnings is a claim on a renewable surplus, while payout supported mainly by the depreciation add-back in operating cash flow is a distribution of the asset base itself, sustainable only until the capital stock must be replaced.
considered.reasoning: This drops the net-external-financing scale leg the critic identified as a published measure and drops the equity-issuance term from the gate, so nothing double-counts financing direction; both tails are firms distributing cash, separated only by the economic character of the cash. It introduces depreciation intensity, a quality variable the archive has never used, and tests capital-consumption rather than market-dependence as the thing that makes payout non-credible.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: UnexpectedRaiseByMatureFirms
considered.expression: MUL(SUB(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at), MA(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at), 5)), RANK(RATIO(re, at)))
considered.hypothesis: For a firm with a deep stock of accumulated earnings, a trip to the capital markets that is large relative to its own five-year financing habit is news — it reveals that internal generation has quietly deteriorated or that management is funding something it cannot justify — whereas the same absolute raise from a habitual issuer is fully expected.
considered.reasoning: Subtracting the firm's own five-year average issuance removes the level of external financing that drives the published anomaly, so a negative slope here cannot simply be a rediscovery of the issuance effect with a different gate — it must come from the surprise component. The construction is two-sided within mature firms (unusual raises at one end, unusual abstention at the other), which activates both legs among established, non-microcap firms and therefore avoids the small-distressed corner where FF5 has repeatedly absorbed the archive's short legs.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: LongLivedInvestmentFundingSurplus
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(at, 1), DELTA(act, 1)), at), INDICATOR(SUB(DELTA(at, 1), DELTA(act, 1)), 0)), WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(oancf, at), RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at)), 1))
considered.hypothesis: The funding-source question bites hardest for irreversible commitments: growth in long-lived, non-current assets cannot be unwound if the cash flow fails to appear, so externally financed fixed-asset expansion is far more likely to be value-destroying than an externally financed build in receivables and inventory, which self-liquidates within a year.
considered.reasoning: The archive winner uses total asset growth, which mixes reversible working-capital swings with irreversible capital commitments; isolating the non-current component identifies the deployment for which management's funding discipline actually matters. If alpha improves, the mechanism is sharpened from "growth" to "irreversible investment," which is a substantive economic refinement rather than a rescaling.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ContractionFundingSurplus
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(NEG(GROWTH(at, 1)), INDICATOR(NEG(GROWTH(at, 1)), 0)), WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(oancf, at), RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at)), 1))
considered.hypothesis: Shrinking the balance sheet also has a funding signature: a firm contracting while running an internal cash surplus is harvesting a mature business and returning capital discipline to shareholders, whereas a firm contracting while still absorbing outside capital is liquidating assets to stay alive.
considered.reasoning: The archive's best signals set every contracting firm to zero, so half the cross-section has never been tested under the funding-source lens and the winner's long-short spread is built only from expanders. This is the natural complement — if it carries independent alpha, a later generation can combine the two halves into a full-coverage signal; if it fails, we learn the mechanism is specific to capital deployment rather than to funding self-sufficiency in general.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: NetMarketDependenceGatedExpansion
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(GROWTH(at, 1), INDICATOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 0)), WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(oancf, at), RATIO(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), ADD(prstkc, dltr)), at)), 1))
considered.hypothesis: What matters for funding credibility is the outside capital a firm actually absorbs on net, not the gross flows it runs through the treasury: a firm that borrows and simultaneously repays, or issues shares while retiring others, has not become market-dependent, whereas gross-flow measures label it as such.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the dividend perturbation the critic correctly called immaterial with a first-order change to the gate's financing leg — gross raising becomes net absorption — which reclassifies exactly the refinancing and churn population the archive has shown behaves differently (DebtRolloverChurn, TwoWayEquityChurn). If the alpha improves, market dependence is about net capital absorbed; if it deteriorates, the gross-flow version is capturing the frictional cost of touching markets at all, which is an equally informative answer.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: SelfFundedExpanderRegime
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(GROWTH(at, 1), INDICATOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 0)), SUB(INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(oancf, at), RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at)), 0), INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at), RATIO(oancf, at)), 0)))
considered.hypothesis: Self-funding is a discrete state rather than a continuous quantity: an expanding firm either covers its growth from operations or it does not, and the market's mistake is failing to classify the firm into the right regime, not mismeasuring by how much the surplus exceeded zero.
considered.reasoning: Rather than crossbreeding two archive members, this asks whether the winner's information lives in the sign or the magnitude of the funding surplus, by replacing the continuous gate with a clean plus-one/minus-one regime classifier while holding the deployment scale fixed. It also directly addresses the outlier sensitivity of the raw-times-raw product the critic flagged in the accepted winner: if a bounded classifier reproduces the alpha, the mechanism is robust regime membership rather than a few extreme surplus observations.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: RaisingRelativeToOwnCashFlowCycle
considered.expression: MUL(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at), ZSCORE(TS_RANK(RATIO(oancf, at), 5)))
considered.hypothesis: A capital raise executed when the firm's own cash flow sits at a five-year high is opportunistic funding of visible opportunity, while the same raise executed at a personal cash-flow trough is filling a hole, and the market does not distinguish the two because both look like ordinary issuance.
considered.reasoning: Cross-sectionally standardizing the within-firm cash-flow percentile centers the gate at zero, so trough-raisers now receive large negative values and peak-raisers large positive ones, repairing the inconsistency where the original expression pushed peak-raisers into the short leg and left trough-raisers indistinguishable from non-issuers. Because the gate is a within-firm timing measure rather than a profitability level, the short leg is populated by ordinarily healthy firms caught at a bad moment rather than by the small-unprofitable corner FF5 already spans.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ExternalCapitalPerUnitOfGrossProfit
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(GROWTH(at, 1), INDICATOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 0)), WINSOR(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), SUB(sale, cogs)), 1))
considered.hypothesis: The right yardstick for market dependence is the firm's own earning engine: raising an amount equal to several years of gross profit to fund expansion is a fundamentally different act from raising a token amount, and expansions requiring large multiples of the margin engine are the ones that disappoint.
considered.reasoning: Expressing the gate as a ratio of financing to gross profit rather than a difference removes the scale-mismatch degeneracy the critic identified — the quantity cannot collapse into gross profitability because the numerator is purely a financing flow — while keeping gross profit's stability advantage over noisy annual cash flow. Gross profit is positive for the overwhelming majority of firms, so the ratio is well behaved without the sign-flip pathology that afflicted earlier cash-flow-denominated coverage ratios.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PureExpanderFundingRegime
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 0), SUB(INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(oancf, at), RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at)), 0), INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at), RATIO(oancf, at)), 0)))
considered.hypothesis: The entire mispricing may be a three-state classification — self-funded expander, market-funded expander, everyone else — with the amount of expansion adding nothing once the funding regime is known.
considered.reasoning: Every strong archive signal still multiplies by continuous asset growth, which means its long leg is tilted toward the most aggressive growers and its spread partly inherits the investment anomaly; removing the magnitude entirely tests whether the funding classification alone carries the alpha. If it does, the resulting signal is fully bounded, essentially immune to outliers and rebalancing lumpiness, and cleanly separable from CMA — the most defensible version of the mechanism to carry into the final generations.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: EquityChannelFundingSurplus
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(GROWTH(at, 1), INDICATOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 0)), WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(oancf, at), RATIO(SUB(sstk, prstkc), at)), 1))
considered.hypothesis: Equity is the informationally sensitive instrument: managers with private good news borrow, and those exploiting rich valuations sell shares, so expansion funded by net equity issuance should be far more damaging than expansion funded by borrowing.
considered.reasoning: The gate has so far pooled equity and debt, leaving unresolved which instrument carries the signal; restricting it to net equity flow isolates the adverse-selection channel and, if it matches or beats the pooled gate, tells us the debt component is dilutive noise. This is a decomposition of a validated mechanism rather than a rescaling, and it also drops the debt-refinancing churn that the archive has repeatedly shown to be mechanical.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: PayoutFundingRegime
considered.expression: MUL(RATIO(ADD(prstkc, dvc), at), SUB(INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(oancf, at), RATIO(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), dltr), at)), 0), INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), dltr), at), RATIO(oancf, at)), 0)))
considered.hypothesis: Distributions carry information only when the distributing firm is genuinely in surplus after its net dealings with capital markets; a firm handing cash to shareholders while absorbing capital elsewhere in the capital structure is recycling investor money and its payout should be discounted entirely.
considered.reasoning: The payout channel has produced modest alphas throughout (1-3.5%) using continuous or rank-based quality gates, and the regime classifier that lifted the expansion signal to a 4.19 t-stat has never been applied to it, so this is a genuine test rather than a restatement. The gate excludes repurchases and dividends from the financing side, so no variable appears on both sides of the interaction and the classification cannot be mechanically induced by the payout itself.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ExternalFundingShareOfExpansion
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 0), WINSOR(RATIO(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), oancf), DELTA(at, 1)), 1))
considered.hypothesis: The economically meaningful quantity is what fraction of this year's balance-sheet growth had to be paid for by outside investors after internal cash was exhausted; growth that required markets to fund most of the increment is systematically overpriced, while growth whose increment was more than covered by operations is underpriced.
considered.reasoning: This is not a crossing of the two tested gates but a change of functional form: because the sort is restricted to expanders, the asset increment is a strictly positive denominator, so the ratio measures the *share* of the deployment financed externally rather than a difference of asset-scaled flows — a scale-free quantity that treats a large firm adding 5% of assets and a small one adding 40% identically. It also avoids the critic's collapse problem, since firms are spread continuously across the ratio instead of being pooled into a dominant plus-one state, with non-expanders sitting at zero between the two economically meaningful tails.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccountingFundsSelfFundedExpansion
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(GROWTH(at, 1), INDICATOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 0)), WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), dvc), at), RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), at)), 1))
considered.hypothesis: Self-funding can be reconstructed entirely from the income statement and balance sheet: retained funds from operations after dividends, measured against the year's increase in debt plus the increase in book equity that earnings did not produce, which is the capital the firm absorbed from outside investors.
considered.reasoning: Both sides of the gate are now scaled by assets, so the expression computes the stated internal-versus-external funding difference in consistent units, repairing the dimensional inconsistency caused by mixing a share-count percentage with asset-scaled flows. The motivation is unchanged and remains the strongest in the batch: every archive gate depends on cash-flow-statement items that cap coverage near 0.08, whereas earnings, depreciation, dividends, debt and book equity are available for a far wider panel, so surviving alpha here buys both robustness and a much larger tradable universe.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: FundingRegimeTransitionExpansion
considered.expression: MUL(INDICATOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 0), SUB(INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(oancf, at), RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at)), 0), INDICATOR(LAG(SUB(RATIO(oancf, at), RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at)), 1), 0)))
considered.hypothesis: The market re-rates funding status slowly, so the return information is concentrated in the year a firm crosses from market dependence into self-funding — it has just proved it can grow on its own cash — and symmetrically in the year a previously self-funded grower first has to reach for outside capital.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the rejected horizon rescaling with a transition mechanism the archive has never tested: differencing the regime classifier removes the persistent level entirely, so the signal cannot be a repackaged investment or profitability anomaly and is instead an event indicator for a change in financial self-sufficiency. It is fully bounded at plus or minus one within expanders, which keeps portfolio membership balanced and immune to outliers while pinpointing the moment at which the mispricing should be corrected.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccountingFundsRegimeExpansion
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(GROWTH(at, 1), INDICATOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 0)), SUB(INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), dvc), at), RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), at)), 0), INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), at), RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), dvc), at)), 0)))
considered.hypothesis: Whether retained funds from operations covered the year's absorption of outside capital is a discrete state, and classifying that state from income-statement and balance-sheet data alone should carry the same information as the cash-flow-statement version while applying to a far larger population of firms.
considered.reasoning: The accounting-funds construction gave the archive's strongest FMB slope (4.85) at coverage 0.126 but only a 2.4% alpha, while in the cash-flow family the switch from a continuous surplus to a sign-only classifier raised the alpha t-stat from 3.74 to 4.19 by removing dependence on a noisy tail of surplus magnitudes. Applying that validated transformation to the high-coverage measure is the single most promising route to a signal that is simultaneously broad, robust, and strong on both metrics.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: FullNetDistributionGatedExpansion
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(GROWTH(at, 1), INDICATOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 0)), WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(oancf, at), RATIO(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), ADD(ADD(prstkc, dvc), dltr)), at)), 1))
considered.hypothesis: A firm's true position versus its capital providers is operating cash flow plus everything it returned to them minus everything it took, and dividends are the largest and most credible component of what is returned — excluding them treats a dividend-paying self-funder as no different from a cash hoarder.
considered.reasoning: The net-absorption gate that added repurchases and debt repayment to the returned side produced the archive's largest alpha (5.6%) and best Sharpe (0.60), so completing the accounting identity with dividends is the natural next lever, and it is an economic completion rather than a rescaling because dividends are typically several times larger than repurchases for mature firms. Comparing it against the existing net gate also tells us whether committed distributions belong in a measure of financial self-sufficiency.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: TurnoverGatedExpansionFunding
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(GROWTH(at, 1), INDICATOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 0)), SUB(RANK(RATIO(sale, at)), RANK(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at))))
considered.hypothesis: The relevant quality dimension may be operating productivity rather than cash generation: a firm whose asset base already produces high revenue per dollar and that expands without outside capital is compounding a proven business model, whereas a low-turnover firm expanding on market money is adding assets it has not shown it can use.
considered.reasoning: Every gate in the winning family measures internal *cash*, leaving open whether the mechanism is specifically about self-financing or more generally about the quality of the firm doing the expanding; asset turnover is a productivity measure with no FF5 counterpart, so a comparable result would broaden the mechanism while a weak one would confirm that cash self-sufficiency is the operative channel. Both legs are expanders, so the contrast remains a funding-and-productivity contrast rather than a growth bet.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: SurplusAndSlackGatedExpansion
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(GROWTH(at, 1), INDICATOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 0)), SUB(RANK(SUB(RATIO(oancf, at), RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at))), RANK(RATIO(lt, at))))
considered.hypothesis: Funding credibility has a flow component and a stock component: expansion is most credible when this year's growth was covered internally *and* the balance sheet retains unused capacity, and least credible when market-funded growth is piled onto an already obligated balance sheet.
considered.reasoning: The archive's early leverage-conditioned signals failed, but they were all attached to issuance intensity rather than to the deployment mechanism that has since proven robust, so the stock dimension has never been tested where the effect actually lives. Adding total liabilities as a second ranked channel introduces balance-sheet slack — a state variable distinct from the flow surplus — and if it improves the alpha it tells us the mispricing concerns funding capacity broadly rather than the current year's cash arithmetic.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ChronicFundingRegimeExpansion
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(GROWTH(at, 1), INDICATOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 0)), MA(SUB(INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(oancf, at), RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at)), 0), INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at), RATIO(oancf, at)), 0)), 3))
considered.hypothesis: Funding self-sufficiency is a durable firm characteristic rather than an annual accident: a firm expanding today after three consecutive years of covering its needs internally is a proven compounder, a firm expanding after three years of continuous market dependence is a serial absorber of outside capital, and firms that switch between the two states carry intermediate information.
considered.reasoning: Averaging the bounded regime classifier over three years yields a two-sided, four-valued measure of chronic funding status, which avoids the degenerate zero mass and the pure asset-growth restatement that the single-state deficit version would have produced. It is also a sharper test of regime persistence than the earlier three-year rank-sum gate: that version smoothed the underlying continuous magnitudes, whereas this counts how many of the last three years the firm actually spent in surplus, which is the economically meaningful notion of a self-financing track record.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: TotalCashCommitmentFundingRegime
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(RATIO(ADD(DELTA(at, 1), ADD(prstkc, dvc)), at), INDICATOR(ADD(DELTA(at, 1), ADD(prstkc, dvc)), 0)), SUB(INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(oancf, at), RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at)), 0), INDICATOR(SUB(RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at), RATIO(oancf, at)), 0)))
considered.hypothesis: The quantity that must be funded is the total cash a firm commits in a year — the dollars added to the balance sheet plus the dollars handed to shareholders — and the credibility of that entire commitment depends on whether operations or capital markets supplied it.
considered.reasoning: This is not a z-score ensemble of two archive signals but a single accounting quantity: asset increase and distributions are both dollar uses of cash scaled by the same denominator, so their sum is dimensionally coherent and their relative weights are the economically correct ones rather than an artificial equalization. It extends the tails to firms that commit cash primarily through distributions rather than growth — including mature payers whose asset base is flat — which should widen the eligible population of both legs relative to the expansion-only construction.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: RetainedFundsFullNetAccountingExpansion
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(GROWTH(at, 1), INDICATOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 0)), WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(ADD(ib, dp), at), RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(ADD(DELTA(ceq, 1), dvc), ib)), at)), 1))
considered.hypothesis: Dividends are evidence of funding strength, not a drain on it: a firm that generated enough funds from operations to expand, service its capital structure and still distribute cash is more self-sufficient than one that merely broke even, so the dividend belongs on the returned side of the identity rather than deducted from internal capacity.
considered.reasoning: In the cash-flow family, moving distributions from the "uses" side to the "returned capital" side lifted alpha from 4.9% to 5.8%, and the current accounting-funds gate does the opposite by subtracting dividends from internal funds — correcting that mistreatment is the most direct route to raising the high-coverage version's alpha from 2.7% toward the cash-flow family's level. The absorbed term still nets repurchases through the change in book equity, so the measure is the complete accounting analogue of the archive's best gate at coverage 0.126.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: FlowAndStockCapacityExpansion
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(GROWTH(at, 1), INDICATOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 0)), SUB(RANK(SUB(RATIO(oancf, at), RATIO(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), ADD(ADD(prstkc, dvc), dltr)), at))), RANK(RATIO(lt, at))))
considered.hypothesis: Credible expansion requires both a flow condition and a stock condition — this year's growth covered by internally generated cash after all dealings with capital providers, and a balance sheet that is not already fully committed to existing claimholders.
considered.reasoning: Slack was shown to be an incremental dimension (SurplusAndSlack reached 5.0% alpha with the cruder gross-flow surplus), and the full-net surplus was shown to be the best flow measure (5.8%); combining the validated flow definition with the validated stock dimension on equal ranked footing is the natural consolidation, and unlike a leverage sort alone the leverage rank here only modulates the funding classification of firms that are actively deploying capital.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: MarginTrajectoryAndFundingExpansion
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(GROWTH(at, 1), INDICATOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 0)), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(SUB(RATIO(oancf, at), RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at)), DELTA(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), at), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Expansion is most credible when the firm both pays for it internally and is simultaneously improving its unit economics; growth funded from markets while gross margins are eroding is the clearest sign that management is buying revenue it cannot make profitable.
considered.reasoning: The level of asset productivity failed to produce alpha (TurnoverGate, 1.3%), but its *direction of change* has never been tested and is a different economic statement — a deteriorating margin trajectory is forward-looking information about the return on the assets being added, whereas a low turnover level is largely a business-model constant. Combining the two ranked channels and centering them keeps the gate two-sided so the sort remains a contrast among expanders rather than a growth bet.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: DilutionAwareFundingExpansion
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(GROWTH(at, 1), INDICATOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 0)), SUB(RANK(SUB(RATIO(oancf, at), RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at))), RANK(GROWTH(csho, 1))))
considered.hypothesis: The cash-flow statement misses a large part of how growth is actually paid for — shares issued in acquisitions and to employees never appear as sstk proceeds — so the change in share count carries funding information beyond the cash surplus, and expansion accompanied by a rising claim base is not self-funded no matter what the cash statement says.
considered.reasoning: Every gate in the winning family measures cash flows only, which means stock-financed acquirers and heavy equity compensators are currently misclassified as self-funded; adding the share-count channel tests whether that misclassification has been costing the signal information. It is a genuine widening of what "external funding" means rather than a rescaling, and the two ranked channels are on identical footing so neither can mechanically dominate.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccountingSurplusAndSlackExpansion
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(GROWTH(at, 1), INDICATOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 0)), SUB(RANK(SUB(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), dvc), at), RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), at))), RANK(RATIO(lt, at))))
considered.hypothesis: The high-coverage accounting measure of self-funding should benefit from the same balance-sheet slack condition as the cash-flow measure: internally funded expansion by a firm with unused capacity is credible, market-funded expansion by an already obligated firm is not.
considered.reasoning: The accounting-funds version delivers the archive's strongest cross-sectional slopes at coverage 0.126 but the weakest alpha of the leading family, and slack is the one modification that has been shown to raise alpha without narrowing the universe, so this pairing is the best candidate for a signal that is simultaneously broad and portfolio-strong. Comparing it against Signal 1 also separates two distinct fixes to the same coverage-rich construction — reclassifying dividends versus adding a stock condition — which is exactly the information the final generation needs.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: UnusualExpansionFundingSurplus
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(SUB(GROWTH(at, 1), MA(GROWTH(at, 1), 5)), INDICATOR(SUB(GROWTH(at, 1), MA(GROWTH(at, 1), 5)), 0)), WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(oancf, at), RATIO(SUB(ADD(sstk, dltis), ADD(ADD(prstkc, dvc), dltr)), at)), 1))
considered.hypothesis: Routine expansion at a firm's habitual pace is already anticipated by investors, so the funding-source question carries the most information when a firm steps up deployment well beyond its own five-year norm: an unusual acceleration paid for from internal cash is a management signal of genuine opportunity, whereas an equally unusual acceleration financed by outside capital is empire-building at the point of maximum overconfidence.
considered.reasoning: Every archive signal has varied the *composition* of the deployment leg (total assets, non-current assets, buybacks, distributions) but never its *unexpectedness*, so this tests a distinct economic claim — that the mispricing is concentrated in deployment surprises — rather than rescaling the same gate as the flagged version did. Benchmarking growth against the firm's own history also strips out the permanent industry and business-model growth differences that make the raw growth scale partly a CMA tilt, so a comparable alpha at lower factor overlap would be a materially cleaner result for the final generation.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AccountingUnusualExpansionFunding
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(SUB(GROWTH(at, 1), MA(GROWTH(at, 1), 5)), INDICATOR(SUB(GROWTH(at, 1), MA(GROWTH(at, 1), 5)), 0)), WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(SUB(ADD(ib, dp), dvc), at), RATIO(ADD(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), SUB(DELTA(ceq, 1), SUB(ib, dvc))), at)), 1))
considered.hypothesis: An unusual step-up in deployment relative to the firm's own history, judged against internal funds reconstructed from the income statement and balance sheet, should carry the same information as the cash-flow version while remaining computable for a far broader panel of firms.
considered.reasoning: The two levers that most need to be combined for a practically usable final signal are the surprise scale (best alpha among gen-8 constructions) and the accounting-funds gate (the only route to coverage 0.126, with the archive's strongest slopes); neither has been paired with the other. A strong result here would give a signal that is broad, low-turnover in its deployment definition, and free of the cash-flow-statement data constraint that has capped the entire archive near 0.08 coverage.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: MaintenanceAdjustedFundingExpansion
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(GROWTH(at, 1), INDICATOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 0)), WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(SUB(oancf, dp), at), RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at)), 1))
considered.hypothesis: Only cash flow in excess of the cost of maintaining the existing asset base can genuinely fund growth; a firm whose entire operating cash flow is consumed by the depreciation of what it already owns is not self-funding its expansion even when the raw surplus looks positive.
considered.reasoning: This is not a factorial recombination of tested gate forms and definitions but a change in what counts as available internal funds — subtracting the maintenance charge before comparing against outside capital — which reclassifies exactly the capital-intensive, high-depreciation firms that the existing gate flatters. Depreciation intensity has been used only once in the archive and never inside the funding gate, so the test isolates whether growth capacity should be measured net of capital consumption.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: OperatingLiabilityFundedExpansion
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(GROWTH(at, 1), INDICATOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 0)), SUB(RANK(SUB(RATIO(oancf, at), RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at))), RANK(DELTA(RATIO(lct, at), 1))))
considered.hypothesis: Capital markets are not the only outside funder of growth: firms also finance expansion by stretching suppliers and accruing obligations, and growth paid for by a swelling current-liability balance is as fragile as growth paid for by issuance, because the claim comes due within the year.
considered.reasoning: Every gate in the archive treats funding as cash flow versus securities issuance, ignoring the operating-liability channel entirely, so this adds a genuinely new funding source rather than re-defining an existing term. The two ranked legs measure different things — cash generated net of securities raised, and the year's build in current obligations — so they complement rather than offset, unlike the dilution pairing the critic rejected.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ProductiveExpansionFundingGap
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(GROWTH(at, 1), INDICATOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 0)), SUB(RANK(SUB(RATIO(oancf, at), RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at))), RANK(SUB(GROWTH(at, 1), GROWTH(sale, 1)))))
considered.hypothesis: Expansion is destructive when assets grow faster than the revenue they generate, and that dilution of productivity is most damaging when outside investors, not operations, paid for the assets; conversely self-funded growth matched by revenue growth is genuine scaling.
considered.reasoning: The gap between asset growth and sales growth is an economically distinct quantity from either the level of turnover (which produced no alpha) or the change in gross margin (which did) — it measures whether the newly added assets are being used at all, independent of pricing and cost structure. Pairing it with the funding surplus asks whether unproductive expansion is penalized specifically when it was externally financed, which is the core interaction hypothesis applied to a new quality dimension.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: ConservativeCashFundedExpansion
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(GROWTH(at, 1), INDICATOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 0)), ZSCORE(SUMRANK(SUB(RATIO(oancf, at), RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at)), RATIO(SUB(oancf, ib), at))))
considered.hypothesis: The credibility of self-funding depends on the credibility of the cash itself: when operating cash flow exceeds reported earnings the surplus reflects conservative accounting and durable collections, whereas a surplus generated alongside earnings that outrun cash is likely to reverse just as the expansion needs financing.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the offsetting dilution pairing with a genuinely orthogonal second channel — the accrual gap — testing whether the *quality* of the internal funds, not just their amount, determines whether market-funded and self-funded expanders separate. Accrual quality has been absent from every gate in the winning family despite being the archive's original quality theme, so a positive result would connect the funding mechanism back to earnings quality rather than restating a net-issuance effect.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: AllChannelFundingCredibility
considered.expression: MUL(MUL(GROWTH(at, 1), INDICATOR(GROWTH(at, 1), 0)), ADD(ZSCORE(RANK(SUB(RATIO(oancf, at), RATIO(ADD(sstk, dltis), at)))), ADD(ZSCORE(RANK(NEG(GROWTH(csho, 1)))), ZSCORE(RANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(lct, at), 1)))))))
considered.hypothesis: A firm can fund growth from three outside sources — securities issuance, new shares handed to sellers and employees, and obligations pushed onto suppliers and accruals — and expansion is credible only when none of them was needed, so the three conditions should be judged with equal standing.
considered.reasoning: The equal weighting the previous version claimed is now actually implemented, since three standardized rank channels are summed directly instead of being nested in a SUMRANK that double-weighted the cash leg. The low-leverage tilt the critic warned about is removed entirely: the third condition is the *change* in current liabilities, a funding flow, rather than a leverage level, so every leg of the gate measures a source of outside funding rather than a balance-sheet quality characteristic.
considered.author: proposer

critic_notes.rationale: This is essentially the product of two heavily documented anomalies (net payout yield and profitability/gross-profitability), and because both legs are non-negative ranks the "interaction" is monotone in each argument, making it a near-linear composite of known factors rather than a state-dependent effect — and its low tail conflates "uninformative" cases with genuine sell signals.

The soft cash-burn gate on gross issuance is a defensible refinement of the external-financing anomaly with sign and expression consistent, though the unranked, highly skewed raw issuance leg risks outlier domination and the cash-flow gate is partly a distress/profitability proxy that FF5 may absorb.

This is a direct rediscovery of the intersection of two canonical anomalies (Sloan accruals and share-issuance/composite-issuance), combined as a monotone rank product that adds no genuine conditioning beyond stacking two same-signed effects.

The signed strain score (leverage rank minus cash-flow rank) genuinely flips the interpretation of net debt flow across states and the expected negative sign is internally consistent for all four quadrants, with the main caveat that the signal collapses toward zero for mid-strain firms so extremes will drive the sort.

Conditioning buybacks on a multi-year cash-flow trend rather than a level is a reasonable and not-quite-standard refinement, but the mass of zero-repurchase firms creates a degenerate, tie-heavy low leg and the 5-year trend window will cost coverage, so the short side may be poorly identified.

Internally inconsistent: because both legs are non-negative ranks, dividend cuts by cash-rich and cash-poor firms both map near zero, so the expression cannot deliver the claimed sign flip for cuts and instead just reproduces a monotone dividend-increase × cash-conversion composite of known effects.

This is a one-knob temporal re-parameterization of the archive's CashBurnFundedExternalFinance (same issuance leg, identical cash-burn gate, only 3-year summing plus winsorizing), so it is a cosmetic variant of an already-evaluated signal and its base leg is the well-documented composite/net external financing anomaly.

The lifecycle (RE/AT) gate is a genuinely different, slower-moving conditioning variable than the archive's cash-flow gates and the sign logic is internally consistent, though both legs individually are well-trodden (issuance anomaly, RE/AT distress-lifecycle) so the incremental content rests entirely on the interaction.

The second-moment gate is an untried conditioning channel and the signed-leg/non-negative-gate construction is coherent with the stated hypothesis (stable firms shrink toward zero rather than flipping), but cash-flow volatility is strongly correlated with size and distress so the gate may end up proxying for those exposures rather than isolating "fragility amplification."

Measuring repurchases as a deviation from the firm's own five-year norm is a substantive fix for the degenerate zero-inflated leg that crippled ImprovingQualityRepurchaser, the gate direction matches the hypothesis, and the two-sided tails give a properly identified sort — main risks are the five-year history requirement eroding coverage and unwinsorized lumpy repurchase spikes.

The financing-mix (pecking-order violation) channel is a real departure from the archive's quantity-based signals, but the finding that the equity component of external financing predicts returns more negatively than the debt component is already established in the net-external-financing decomposition literature, and the expression does not actually condition on raising capital as the hypothesis claims (it relies on rank ties at zero to do so implicitly).

Sign logic is internally consistent and the non-negative two-channel SUMRANK gate is a defensible diagnosis-driven fix for the collapsed signed gate in LeverageStrainedDebtIssuance, but the base leg is just the sign-flipped net debt issuance measure from that same archive entry, so the test is closer to a re-parameterization than a new channel and will likely be highly correlated with it.

The second term is verbatim the archive's CashBurnFundedExternalFinance and the first is PayoutCredibilityGate with RANK swapped for IND_ZSCORE, so this is a mechanical linear recombination of two already-tested signals rather than a new mechanism, and the well-behaved -2.8 t-stat leg will likely just be diluted by the weak payout leg.

The retrenchment (change-based) angle is a genuinely fresh cut on the payout theme and the cut-plus-cash-stress tail matches the negative expected sign, but the hypothesis's second clause is internally inconsistent — a dividend *increase* by a cash-poor firm produces a large negative signal value, which under a negative expected sign predicts outperformance, the opposite of the claimed "unsustainable bluff."

Share-count growth is itself a heavily published anomaly (Pontiff-Woodgate, composite issuance) so much of any result will be a rediscovery, but gating it on the *change* in asset turnover rather than a profitability level is a defensible and sign-consistent cross-theme construction worth one test.

Using the firm's own five-year leverage position to identify debt-capacity exhaustion is a real distinction from the archive's cross-sectional leverage ranks and the sign is coherent, though the non-negative intensity gate makes it structurally close to IssuanceAgainstDepletedRetainedEarnings and risks reproducing that signal's fmb/alpha sign conflict.

Contrasting internally funded against debt-funded repurchases is an economically sensible signed gate that genuinely activates the short leg, but the claim of orthogonality to RMW is overstated since RANK(oancf/at) is a profitability rank, and the zero-inflated prstkc base that weakened ImprovingQualityRepurchaser is unaddressed.

The stated mechanism contradicts the expression — RANK(oancf/at) is non-negative, so cash-poor diluters (the claimed short leg) are shrunk toward zero while the most negative values are dilution by *high* cash-flow firms — and beyond that it is essentially ImprovingQualityRepurchaser with csho substituted for prstkc layered on the published net-share-issuance anomaly.

This is essentially the archive's best signal (BuybackFundingSource) with both legs mechanically broadened — payout to prstkc+dvc (already tested as PayoutCredibilityGate) and financing to sstk+dltis — so it reads as a cosmetic union of two archived constructs rather than a new mechanism, and the smooth, persistent dividend level will likely dominate the payout scale and pull the sort toward the known payout-yield anomaly.

Extending the funding-source contrast to gross debt retirement is a genuinely different financing action with a coherent nonnegative-scale × signed-gate construction, though the gate alone (high operating cash flow minus high equity issuance) is close to a known profitability-plus-issuance composite, so much of any resulting alpha may be a rescaled version of well-documented effects.

The ratio is non-monotone and unstable whenever five-year operating cash flow is negative or close to offsetting cumulative issuance (denominator can approach zero or turn negative, flipping the sign for the most distressed firms that the signal is supposed to short), and once winsorized it is largely a monotone repackaging of the well-known external-financing/net-issuance anomaly scaled by cash-flow profitability.

The mechanism — issuance conditioned on accrual quality — is the same one already tested as DilutionQualityGate (with the sign merely reversed by using ib−oancf instead of oancf−ib), and because every factor in the product is nonnegative and the indicator zeroes out all unprofitable firms, the long leg becomes a large tied mass of zeros rather than an economically identified group.

Rollover volume via MIN(issuance, retirement) is a quantity that all net-debt-flow signals mechanically cancel and the working-capital gate is a balance-sheet liquidity dimension absent from FF5, making this a substantively new test, though it inherits the structural fragility seen in the archived MIN-based churn signal and the working-capital gate will pick up strong industry/business-model tilts.

Multiplying a signed dividend change by a signed funding-source gate makes the sign economically incoherent in one quadrant: firms cutting dividends while heavily tapping outside capital (negative × negative) land in the long leg, and internally funded cutters land in the short leg, which directly contradicts the stated credibility mechanism.

The two summed scale legs are on wildly different scales (annual asset growth is O(0.1–1) while prstkc/at is O(0.01)), so the composite will be numerically dominated by asset growth and end up a near-duplicate of the archive's ExpansionFundingSource rather than the claimed "breadth" test.

A legitimate single-lever ablation that replaces the rank-difference gate with the economically literal funding surplus and thereby diagnoses whether the winner's alpha comes from measured self-funding or from an embedded profitability (RMW-like) rank, though its novelty is limited and the raw-times-raw product will be outlier-sensitive despite the winsorization.

Swapping RANK for IND_RANK in an existing strong signal is a standard mechanical neutralization rather than a substantively different mechanism, and the archive already contains industry-conditioned gates (IND_ZSCORE), so the expected information gain is cosmetic.

The scale leg (dividends + buybacks + net debt retirement, scaled by assets) is essentially the sign-flipped Bradshaw–Richardson–Sloan net-external-financing / total-payout measure, so the signal risks rediscovering a published anomaly dressed in a gate that itself re-uses equity issuance and thus double-counts financing direction.

Genuinely explores financing-policy instability rather than level and pairs it with an untried quality dimension, but the 5-year volatility of scaled net financing is mechanically tied to size/age and the gate is literally negated Novy-Marx gross profitability, so a strong result may be a size-times-known-profitability composite rather than the proposed mechanism.

Since the same issuance scale with the opposite retained-earnings gate already produced a strongly negative FMB slope in the archive, a negative slope here would most likely just reflect the base external-financing anomaly rather than the claimed "unexpected raise by mature firms" channel, making the two gate directions mutually uninformative.

Decomposing the deployment term into its irreversible non-current component is a genuine economic sharpening of the archive's best mechanism (not a rescaling), the two ratio terms are on comparable scales so the funding gate retains bite, and the sign convention is internally consistent — though the non-current-growth leg does overlap the well-known investment/asset-growth anomaly, so any gain must come from the interaction rather than the level.

Testing the untouched contracting half of the cross-section under the same funding-source gate is a legitimate and diagnostically informative complement with a coherent sign, but it inherits the archive's structural weakness of assigning exact zeros to the majority (expanders), so the long-short spread will be driven by a small, potentially unstable liquidating-firm tail and the "harvesting vs. liquidating" reading is economically looser than the expansion case.

Subtracting common dividends from operating cash flow perturbs the gate by roughly one to two percent of assets against an oancf/at term an order of magnitude larger, so this is a near-monotone rescaling of RawSurplusGatedExpansion that will almost certainly reproduce its results, and the framing of dividends as an "unavoidable commitment" reducing quality also cuts against their usual positive quality signal.

This is a mechanical crossbreed of two already-evaluated archive members whose outcome will most likely interpolate between them, and mixing a unit-free SUMRANK scale with a raw dollar-scaled gate reintroduces exactly the tail-dilution/magnitude tension the proposal claims to resolve, so it adds little new economic content beyond a hill-climbing step.

The expression is internally inconsistent with its hypothesis: since TS_RANK is non-negative, the signal is weakly negative everywhere, placing large raisers at their own cash-flow *peaks* in the short leg while trough-raisers are numerically indistinguishable from the mass of non-issuers at zero — the reverse of the stated mechanism, and what remains is close to the known gross-issuance anomaly.

Gross profit/assets is typically several times larger than issuance/assets, so the "surplus" difference collapses to gross profitability and the signal degenerates into asset growth × gross profitability — a well-known quality-growth combination largely spanned by the RMW and CMA legs of the FF5 benchmark — thereby discarding the funding-source mechanism the proposal claims to test.

This is a mechanical crossing of two already-tested archive variants (SelfFundedExpanderRegime's sign gate and NetMarketDependenceGatedExpansion's net-flow measure) with a predictable outcome, and substituting net for gross financing inside a binary gate will push the large majority of firms into the +1 state (any firm with positive oancf and non-positive net issuance), collapsing the discriminating power the gross-flow gate had.

Stripping the continuous asset-growth scale is a genuine and well-motivated diagnostic — it directly tests whether the archive's alphas are the funding classification or a repackaged investment/CMA tilt — though the resulting three-valued signal will produce massive ties that make quantile sorts and the FMB slope coarse, so the interpretation must be as a clean regime spread rather than a smooth signal.

The instrument decomposition is a legitimate test of the adverse-selection channel, but note that oancf minus net equity issuance embeds the well-known net-share-issuance/repurchase anomaly directly in the gate (repurchases now *raise* the surplus score), so a positive result will be hard to separate from net share issuance interacted with asset growth rather than evidence about funding credibility.

The coverage motivation is the best in this batch, but the funding-need term is dimensionally inconsistent — RATIO(DELTA(debt),at) is a change scaled by assets while GROWTH(csho,1) is a unitless percentage change that will typically dominate it in magnitude — so the expression does not compute the stated "internal funds versus external funds absorbed" quantity and any result would be uninterpretable without rescaling share issuance to assets.

Applying the binary surplus classifier to the payout channel is a defensible untested combination, but it is conceptually close to PayoutCredibilityGate/PayoutCoverageStrain (a payout signal gated on free-cash-flow adequacy, a channel that has repeatedly produced weak alphas here), and the gate's asymmetric treatment of dltr but not prstkc is an awkward inconsistency even if it avoids double-counting.

Replacing one-year asset growth with a three-year cumulative sum in the scaling leg of SelfFundedExpanderRegime is a horizon rescaling of the deployment magnitude rather than a new mechanism, and multi-year cumulative asset growth is itself a documented investment anomaly, so a positive result would be hard to attribute to the funding-regime insight.

A coherent and internally consistent cross of two independently validated archive ingredients (the high-coverage accounting-funds surplus and the sign-only regime classifier, with expansion magnitude retained so the PureExpander degeneracy is avoided), though it is a derivative refinement whose main contribution is coverage rather than new economics.

Once the self-funded leg is removed the signal collapses to "asset growth among externally financed firms," which is close to a direct restatement of the asset-growth and net-external-financing anomalies, and because the variable is zero for every non-expanding and every self-funded firm the sort has a huge mass point at zero that makes the short/neutral legs degenerate — the same portfolio-instability failure the reasoning claims to repair.

This is a mechanical z-score ensemble of two already-tested archive signals whose result is largely predictable from their parents, and its stated motivation is factually wrong — DualChannelDeploymentFundingSource used SUMRANK, which already standardizes both channels by rank, so "asset growth dominated a smaller payout term" was not the failure mode being fixed.

Adding dividends to the returned side completes the standard net-external-financing identity, so the extension is economically coherent and sign-consistent with the archive's best gate, but it is a one-term increment on an already strong signal and risks simply loading on a dividend-payer tilt, which the follow-up must diagnose.

This substitutes a genuinely different gate — asset productivity rather than internal cash — onto the proven deployment mechanism, making it a real discriminating test rather than a cosmetic variant, with the caveat that unadjusted sale/at ranks carry heavy industry composition that should be checked.

The flow-versus-stock distinction is a legitimate untested dimension of the winning mechanism and the expression's direction matches the stated hypothesis, but RANK(lt/at) is nearly the complement of book leverage and thus overlaps known leverage/distress effects, so any improvement will need to be shown incremental to a simple leverage control.

The algebra is internally consistent (the absorbed term Δceq+dvc−ib correctly isolates net equity issuance, so adding dvc back to internal funds is a clean reclassification of dividends to the "returned" side, exactly analogous to the cash-flow family's 4.9%→5.8% improvement), but the change amounts to an additive +dvc/at shift in an already-tested gate and therefore risks simply importing a dividend-payer/payout-yield tilt rather than sharpening the funding-regime classification.

ZSCORE(RANK(x)) is a monotone re-scaling of the same full-net surplus gate already tested in FullNetDistributionGatedExpansion, so this is a cosmetic functional-form variant, and the stated motivation — that the sign classifier "becomes degenerate once returns are netted" — is speculation, since the full-net sign classifier was never run and the gross-flow version scored the archive's best ls_talpha (4.19).

A legitimate but highly predictable consolidation — it is SurplusAndSlackGatedExpansion with the gross-flow surplus swapped for the validated full-net surplus — and the leverage-rank subtraction may simply dilute the stronger flow signal rather than add an independent stock dimension, since the full-net surplus already embeds dltis and dltr.

Margin trajectory is a genuinely untested and economically distinct channel (level of turnover ≠ change in gross profitability), and the construction is coherent and two-sided, but Δ(gross profit/assets) is close to the published change-in-gross-profitability anomaly so the composite may load on that standalone effect, and the proposal inconsistently reverts to the inferior gross-flow surplus after arguing the full-net version is better.

This is the most substantive proposal in the batch because share-count growth captures non-cash funding (stock acquisitions, equity compensation) that every prior gate in the family structurally omits, though the reviewer should verify the result is not simply asset growth crossed with the well-known net-share-issuance anomaly rather than a true funding-regime interaction.

Applying the validated slack condition to the high-coverage accounting-funds gate is a reasonable and diagnostically useful pairing against Signal 1, but it is the same mechanical crossing as Signal 3 with partially redundant leverage information (the absorbed term already contains Δ(dltt+dlc) while the slack rank uses lt/at), and its incremental content over the existing family is thin.

This is a pure factorial recombination of two archive signals (SelfFundedExpanderRegime's sign gate with FullNetDistributionGatedExpansion's surplus definition) with no new economic content, and since the classifier is bounded at ±1 essentially all cross-sectional dispersion comes from the asset-growth magnitude leg — i.e. the signal is largely a sign-conditioned asset-growth anomaly, which the archive's PureExpanderFundingRegime result (fmb +3.82 but ls_alpha −0.033) already warns about.

Another one-lever swap in the same 2x2 (surprise-scaled deployment already tested at 5.3%/t=3.71 with the continuous full-net gate; the sign gate already tested with gross flows), and it inherits the same problem that a ±1 gate leaves the deployment surprise doing all the ranking work, so the incremental information over its two parents is minimal.

The clearest practical motivation of the six — pairing the within-firm deployment surprise with the balance-sheet reconstruction of internal funds addresses the family's binding coverage constraint rather than reshuffling gate forms — though the 5-year MA on asset growth will claw back part of the promised 0.126 coverage and the construction remains an incremental variant of two well-tested archive components.

Identical to MarginTrajectoryAndFundingExpansion except the surplus term is redefined from gross to net flows — a single-term substitution whose expected effect (a modest shift in one of two equally ranked composite legs) is too small to constitute a substantively different hypothesis.

A cosmetic swap of the surplus definition inside the already-tested DilutionAwareFundingExpansion, and the two legs now partially offset rather than complement — the full-net surplus rewards repurchases while the csho-growth rank penalizes issuance, so both legs load on the same net-equity-issuance dimension that the share-issuance anomaly literature already spans.

Internally inconsistent with its own stated design — the nested SUMRANK gives the cash-surplus leg roughly double the weight of slack and dilution rather than the claimed "equally weighted ranks" — and the NEG(lt/at) leg imports a plain low-leverage/quality tilt that risks driving any measured alpha independently of the funding mechanism.

validation_diagnostics.message: proposal expression does not use any variable exclusive to required theme: financing (variables shared across the paired themes, e.g. common denominators like 'at', do not count as evidence for either theme)
